### Questions

These are the data we collected in class from the first two experiments. In the first,
each of you answered 14 trivia questions with a range that you were 90% sure contained
the right answer. In the second, you saw 20 words, one at a time, and then wrote down as
many as you could remember.

For the first experiment, `question` has the text and the correct `answer` for each of
the 14 questions. `guess` has one row per person per question, with the low and high
ends of the range in `guess_low` and `guess_high`. `people` has a few facts about each
person: `height` in inches, whether they have `watched_friends`, whether they
`plays_basketball`, and their `major`. Heights and the basketball hoop are in inches;
answers written in centimeters, and hoop guesses of 30 or more with no unit, have
been converted.

For the second experiment, `word` has the 20 words, with the `position` each word was
shown in and a few features of the word. `recall` has one row for each word a person
wrote down, and `mem_people` has the class year and whether each person is bilingual.

Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it
to a variable.

1. Start with a warm-up. Filter `guess` to question 11 (the average height of an adult
man) and sort by `guess_low`.

```{python}
(
    guess
    .filter(c.question == 11)
    .sort(c.guess_low)
)
```

2. Draw a scatter plot from `people` with `height` on the x-axis and `major` on the
y-axis.

```{python}
(
    people
    .ggplot(aes(c.height, c.major))
    .geom_point()
)
```

3. Now the first experiment. Join `question` onto `guess` and add a column `hit` that is
true when the `answer` is between `guess_low` and `guess_high`. You can write this as
`(c.answer >= c.guess_low) & (c.answer <= c.guess_high)`.

```{python}
(
    guess
    .join(question, on=c.question)
    .with_columns(
        hit = (c.answer >= c.guess_low) & (c.answer <= c.guess_high)
    )
)
```

4. Take the code from the previous question and compute the mean of `hit` across all of
the rows. The mean of a true/false column is the proportion of rows that are true.

```{python}
(
    guess
    .join(question, on=c.question)
    .with_columns(
        hit = (c.answer >= c.guess_low) & (c.answer <= c.guess_high)
    )
    .select(hit = c.hit.mean())
)
```

If everyone had given honest 90% ranges, about 90% of them would contain the answer.
Only 41% did. The ranges were far too narrow: as a class, we were much more sure of
ourselves than we should have been.

5. Take the code from question 3, group by `question`, and compute the mean of `hit`.
Draw a bar plot with `question` on the x-axis and the mean on the y-axis, and add
`.geom_hline(yintercept=0.9, linetype="dashed")` to draw a line at 90%.

```{python}
(
    guess
    .join(question, on=c.question)
    .with_columns(
        hit = (c.answer >= c.guess_low) & (c.answer <= c.guess_high)
    )
    .group_by(c.question)
    .agg(hit = c.hit.mean())
    .ggplot(aes(c.question, c.hit))
    .geom_col()
    .geom_hline(yintercept=0.9, linetype="dashed")
)
```

Only the coffee question (6) and the height of an adult man (11) come close to the line.
The worst are Charlemagne (5) and the number of words on the front page of the New York
Times (13).

6. A miss can be too high or too low. Take the code from question 3, group by
`question`, and compute `too_high`, the mean of `c.guess_low > c.answer`, and
`too_low`, the mean of `c.guess_high < c.answer`. Sort by `question`.

```{python}
(
    guess
    .join(question, on=c.question)
    .with_columns(
        hit = (c.answer >= c.guess_low) & (c.answer <= c.guess_high)
    )
    .group_by(c.question)
    .agg(
        too_high = (c.guess_low > c.answer).mean(),
        too_low = (c.guess_high < c.answer).mean()
    )
    .sort(c.question)
)
```

Charlemagne was crowned in 800, and 86% of the ranges were entirely later than that.
For the number of words a person speaks in a day (14), 73% of the ranges were too low.
The misses are not random noise; on most questions, the class leaned the same way.

7. Now look at people instead of questions. Take the code from question 3, group by
`name`, compute the number of hits with `c.hit.sum()`, and sort from the most hits to
the fewest.

```{python}
(
    guess
    .join(question, on=c.question)
    .with_columns(
        hit = (c.answer >= c.guess_low) & (c.answer <= c.guess_high)
    )
    .group_by(c.name)
    .agg(hits = c.hit.sum())
    .sort(c.hits, descending=True)
)
```

A well-calibrated person would get about 12 or 13 of the 14 questions. The best in the
class got 10, and most people got between 4 and 7.

8. Did people who have watched *Friends* do better on the two *Friends* questions (8
and 9)? Take the code from question 3, join `people` onto it, filter to questions 8 and
9, group by `question` and `watched_friends`, and compute the mean of `hit` and the
number of rows. Sort by `question`.

```{python}
(
    guess
    .join(question, on=c.question)
    .with_columns(
        hit = (c.answer >= c.guess_low) & (c.answer <= c.guess_high)
    )
    .join(people, on=c.name)
    .filter(c.question.is_in([8, 9]))
    .group_by(c.question, c.watched_friends)
    .agg(
        hit = c.hit.mean(),
        n = pl.len()
    )
    .sort(c.question, c.watched_friends)
)
```

Not in any way we can see. Viewers did a little worse on question 8 and a little better
on question 9, but with only 8 viewers, one person changes their rate by more than 12
points. The join also dropped JAM, who is in `guess` but not in `people`.

9. Do taller people guess that the average man is taller? Filter `guess` to question 11,
join `people`, and add a column `mid` with the middle of the range,
`(c.guess_low + c.guess_high) / 2`. Draw a scatter plot of `mid` against `height`.

```{python}
(
    guess
    .filter(c.question == 11)
    .join(people, on=c.name)
    .with_columns(mid = (c.guess_low + c.guess_high) / 2)
    .ggplot(aes(c.height, c.mid))
    .geom_point()
)
```

There is no clear pattern. Almost every range is centered between 67 and 73 inches,
whatever the height of the person guessing.

10. Now the second experiment. As a warm-up, count the number of words each person
wrote down in `recall` and sort from the fewest to the most.

```{python}
(
    recall
    .group_by(c.name)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .sort(c.n)
)
```

11. Some of the responses were not on the list. Use an anti join of `recall` with `word`
to find them. The keys have different names, so use `left_on=c.response` and
`right_on=c.word`.

```{python}
(
    recall
    .join(word, left_on=c.response, right_on=c.word, how="anti")
)
```

Three people remembered a word that they never saw. Psychologists call these
intrusions. "Glass" fits in with "bottle" and "window", and "color" fits with "yellow".

12. Count the number of people who recalled each word: group `recall` by `response` and
count the rows. Then join `word` onto the result and sort by `position`.

```{python}
(
    recall
    .group_by(c.response)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .join(word, left_on=c.response, right_on=c.word)
    .sort(c.position)
)
```

13. Take the code from the previous question and draw a line plot of `n` against
`position`, with points on top of the line.

```{python}
(
    recall
    .group_by(c.response)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .join(word, left_on=c.response, right_on=c.word)
    .sort(c.position)
    .ggplot(aes(c.position, c.n))
    .geom_line()
    .geom_point()
)
```

This is called a serial position curve. The first six words were recalled by most of
the 17 people, and recall drops after that, apart from "yellow"; memory researchers call
this the primacy effect. The spike at position 14 is the one vulgar word, which all 17 people
remembered.

14. Take the code from question 12 and group the result by `in_room`, computing the mean
of `n`. Was a word easier to remember when the object was in the room with us?

```{python}
(
    recall
    .group_by(c.response)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .join(word, left_on=c.response, right_on=c.word)
    .group_by(c.in_room)
    .agg(n = c.n.mean())
)
```

No. The words for objects in the room were recalled by 10.8 people on average, and the
other words by 11.3.

15. Last, the people. Take the code from question 10, join `mem_people` onto it, group
by `bilingual`, and compute the mean of `n` and the number of people.

```{python}
(
    recall
    .group_by(c.name)
    .agg(n = pl.len())
    .join(mem_people, on=c.name)
    .group_by(c.bilingual)
    .agg(
        n_mean = c.n.mean(),
        people = pl.len()
    )
)
```

The bilingual students recalled about one more word on average (14.0 against 12.6), but
there are only 13 people here. Four people who did the memory task are not in
`mem_people`, so the join dropped them.

16. Last question, and it is a written one. Pick one of the results above and describe
how you would change the experiment to get a more convincing answer.

**Answer**: For example, the *Friends* comparison in question 8 has only two questions
and 21 people. A better version would ask several more *Friends* questions and compare
viewers and non-viewers on all of them, ideally with more people.
